title: Distinct values in many ranges
prompt: Write countDistinctInRanges(nums []int, queries [][2]int) []int returning, for each query {l, r} (inclusive, 0-indexed), how many distinct values sit in nums[l..r]. Answers must come back in the order the queries were given. The tests run 600000 queries over 200000 values, so re-scanning each range is out; you are free to answer the queries in whatever order you like as long as you re-index the results.
explanation: Distinct-count has no subtractive structure: knowing the answers for [0, r] and [0, l-1] tells you nothing about [l, r], so a prefix array does not exist and a segment tree has nothing to combine. What does exist is cheap incremental maintenance: given the answer for a window, extending or shrinking it by one position costs O(1) with a count-per-value array (a value's count going 0 to 1 adds one distinct, 1 to 0 removes one). Mo's algorithm is what turns that into an algorithm: sort the queries by (l/block, r), then walk one window across all of them. The left pointer moves at most block per query, so q*block in total, and the right pointer sweeps at most n within each block, so (n/block)*n in total. Setting block to sqrt(n) balances the two at O((n + q) * sqrt(n)). Two details matter. Sorting the right endpoint in alternating directions per block (ascending in even blocks, descending in odd) halves the right pointer's travel and is free to write. And the add/remove pair must be exact inverses: it is very easy to write a remove that decrements after the zero check, which drifts the count and only shows up on the large tests. The alternative that also passes is the offline BIT sweep, sorting queries by r and keeping a 1 at each value's most recent occurrence, which is O((n + q) log n); reach for it when you need better than sqrt, and for Mo's when the per-element statistic is something a BIT cannot maintain.
hints: Answers for [0, r] and [0, l-1] cannot be subtracted here. What can you do cheaply instead, given the answer for one window and a window one position wider?
If you may answer the queries in any order, which order makes the two window endpoints travel least in total?
With the left endpoint pinned to a block of width B, how far does the right endpoint travel across all the queries in that block?

title: Maximum bipartite matching
prompt: Write maxBipartiteMatching(n, m int, adj [][]int) int returning the size of a maximum matching between left vertices 0..n-1 and right vertices 0..m-1, where adj[u] lists the right vertices left vertex u may be paired with. Each vertex may be used at most once. Greedy in index order is wrong: the tests include graphs where an early pairing has to be moved aside to fit a later one.
explanation: The one idea is the augmenting path: a path that starts at an unmatched left vertex, alternates unmatched and matched edges, and ends at an unmatched right vertex. Flipping every edge along it raises the matching by exactly one, because the path has one more unmatched edge than matched. Berge's theorem says a matching is maximum precisely when no augmenting path exists, which is what makes 'try each unmatched left vertex once and keep it if it augments' correct rather than merely greedy. Kuhn's algorithm is that search written as a DFS: for left vertex u, walk its right neighbours, and take v if v is free or if v's current partner can itself be re-routed. The critical detail is the visited marker. It must be per augmentation attempt, not per recursion frame, or the search revisits a right vertex through a different partner and loops forever; the usual bug is stamping the marker with the current left vertex instead of the root of the search. Each attempt is O(E), so the whole thing is O(V*E), which is fine to a few thousand vertices; Hopcroft-Karp finds a maximal set of shortest augmenting paths per phase and gets O(E*sqrt(V)) when that is not enough. The greedy pre-pass is not needed for correctness but usually places most of the matching for free, leaving augmentation only the hard cases. Worth remembering alongside this: Koenig's theorem makes maximum matching equal to minimum vertex cover on a bipartite graph, so 'minimum rows and columns to cover all the ones' and 'maximum independent set' both reduce to this function.
hints: If every right vertex a left vertex can reach is already taken, is that left vertex necessarily hopeless?
Describe a path that starts unmatched, ends unmatched, and alternates. What happens to the matching size if you flip every edge on it?
When your search backtracks into a right vertex a second time during the same attempt, what should happen? What exactly does the marker have to be stamped with?
refs: LC 2172 Maximum AND Sum of Array

title: Sample k items from a stream
prompt: Write reservoirSample(next func() (int, bool), k int, r *rand.Rand) []int returning k values drawn uniformly at random, without replacement, from the stream that next yields until it reports false. The length of the stream is not known in advance and you get one pass over it; return everything if the stream is shorter than k. Use r for every random choice. The tests check that each element of a 100-element stream survives close to k/100 of the time over 60000 runs, so a scheme that is merely random is not enough: it has to be uniform.
explanation: Fill the reservoir with the first k values, then for the i-th value (1-indexed) keep it with probability k/i, evicting a uniformly chosen one of the k already held. The induction is short: assume every one of the first i-1 values is in the reservoir with probability k/(i-1). Value i enters with probability k/i. An older value survives if either i is skipped (probability 1 - k/i) or i enters but evicts one of the other k-1 slots (probability (k/i) * (k-1)/k), which together give (i-1)/i, and (k/(i-1)) * ((i-1)/i) = k/i. So after the whole stream every element is held with probability k/n. Writing that as 'draw j = r.Intn(i) and replace slot j when j < k' does both coin flips in one call, since j < k happens with probability k/i and j is uniform on the slots when it does. The two ways to get it wrong are both visible in the distribution rather than in a crash: replacing a random slot unconditionally on every element (r.Intn(k)) makes the last k elements the only possible survivors, and an off-by-one in the range (r.Intn(i+1), or counting before incrementing) tilts the whole stream one way. Note what the tests cannot check: buffering the entire stream and shuffling is also uniform and would pass, so the O(k) space bound is the point of the technique rather than something the grader enforces. The k = 1 case is the interview classic (pick a random node from a linked list of unknown length), and weighting the acceptance probability by w_i / running_total generalises it to a weighted sample.
hints: You cannot know n until the stream ends, but you can decide about element i when you see it. What probability must that decision use so that the answer is still uniform at the end?
When you decide to keep a new element, which of the ones you are already holding should go, and why does it have to be chosen uniformly?
Can a single call to r.Intn make both decisions at once? What range would it need?
refs: Vitter, Random Sampling with a Reservoir
